title: Britain's "missing link" was a fake. In December 1912 Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward
description:
In December 1912 Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward presented Piltdown Man to the Geological Society. It was billed as an early human ancestor.

Waterston in 1913 and Boule in 1915 argued it was an ape jaw with a human skull. Both were dismissed for decades.

Tests in 1953 showed the jaw and teeth were not the same age as the skull, and the jaw was most likely an orangutan's. The skull was human and far more recent than claimed.

From the 1912 announcement to the 1953 exposure.

A 2016 study found one forger's methods throughout, and named Dawson.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piltdown_Man (read): established that Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward presented the find on 18 December 1912, that doubts were raised within a few years (Waterston 1913, Boule 1915), that fluorine absorption tests by Oakley, Le Gros Clark and Weiner exposed it in 1953, and that the pieces combined a medieval human skull with an orangutan jaw and filed teeth.
- https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/aso/databank/entries/do53pi.html (read): established that the hoax was reported on 21 November 1953 after the Natural History Museum published its findings, that an improved fluorine test showed the jaw and teeth were not the same age as the skull, and that the jaw was most likely an orangutan's.
- https://nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2016/august/piltdown-man-charles-dawson-likely-fraudster.html (read): established that a 2016 study found consistent working methods pointing to one forger, Charles Dawson, and that DNA linked teeth from two sites to the same orangutan.
